newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Celltech says share drop overdone.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Celltech says share drop overdone.

text.p: Celltech Group Plc said on Wednesday it was surprised at the scale of the drop in its share price in the wake of news that two lead drugs for septic shock had been abandoned.

In a telephone interview with Reuters, finance director Peter Allen said analysts had been valuing BAYX-1351, which partner Bayer AG said it had dropped because of disappointing trial results, and its follow-up drug CAP-571 at between 200 and 400 pence per share.
"I think that clearly the (share price) yesterday of 630 pence did not assume success for septic shock, so there is surprise at the scale of the reaction."
Shares in the group were down 54 percent in midmorning trading at 287 1/2 pence.

Allen told Reuters that the company did not know until Tuesday that Phase III trials in the U.S. of BAYX-1351 had shown no effect on cutting death rates in patients with septic shock, a poisoning of the body which sets in after major surgery or trauma.
"They had made encouraging noises over the past few months so it was as great a surprise to them as to us."
He said Bayer had made "a very significant investment," in the product, including stockpiling supplies of the drug and investing in manufacturing capacity in California.
Bayer, which carried the costs of developing the drug, also paid Celltech non-returnable milestones of 15.7 million stg.
Allen said earlier trials had shown the drug reduced mortality rates by 17.4 percent at 28 days.

Celltech was due to have exclusive rights to sell a successful product in Britain, France and Ireland, and the company told Reuters in January that it could have achieved peak annual sales in those three markets of $75 million.
The failure of the drug means follow-up drug CDP-571, which uses human antibodies developed by Celltech, would not be pursued for the condition.

Allen said the group would now pursue CDP-571 itself for Crohn's disease, a poorly treated disease affecting the small intestine, and possibly for rheumatoid arthritis, although "this is commercially not as interesting as Crohn's."
He said a small-scale intermediate, or Phase II, trial had shown "significant reduction in the disease."
"We believe we have got a very encouraging pipeline," Allen said.

Work is proceeding on a drug for acute leukaemia, CMA-676, with American Home Products Corp. He said an update on the drug at the American Society of Clinical Oncology conference last week was viewed by analysts as "further encouraging news."
The companies hope the drug, which uses a Celltech antibody to target cancer cells with an AHP cell-killing product, could replace chemotherapy as a treatment.
"We believe we should get an expedited review by the FDA (U.S. Food and Drug Administration)," he said.
Celltech and AHP are also undertaking trials on an ovarian cancer drug this year, and a trial for small-cell lung cancer is due to start in the UK this year.
A product to treat psoriasis, CDP-850, is due to start placebo-controlled Phase II trials.

Allen also underlined a number of other collaborations, including its search with Merck & Co for a compound to go into clinical trials for treatment of asthma. "We hope that something will be decided during the second half of the year," he said.
Zeneca Group Plc is working with Celltech on looking at MMP inhibitors, primarily for treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, although work on a chosen compound is "not scheduled before next year."
-- Jonathan Birt, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
